cse-2012-cs-40.approach: Run Dijkstra exactly as specified and track the **predecessor** of every vertex. Ties matter here: a distance (and its predecessor) changes only when a *strictly* shorter path appears, so the path reported to T is whichever path first set $d(T)$ to its final value.
cse-2012-cs-40.given: Directed edges (weight): S→A 4, S→B 3, S→D 7, B→S 3, B→D 4, A→C 1, C→D 3, C→E 1, D→E 1, D→T 3, D→F 5, E→G 2, G→E 2, E→T 4, G→T 3, T→F 5. Source S, target T.

steps.title: Initialise the distances
steps.body: $d(S)=0$ and every other $d(v)=\infty$. The priority queue holds only S.

steps.title: Extract S (0) and relax its edges
Extract B (3): B→D ties, so nothing changes
steps.body: B→S leads to a finished vertex. Through B, $d(D)$ would be $3+4=7$, which is **not strictly less** than the current $7$, so D keeps predecessor S.

steps.title: Extract C (5): improve E, not D
steps.body:
- $d(E) = 5+1 = 6$, pred E = C (new)
- via C, D would get $5+3 = 8 > 7$ — no change.

steps.title: Extract E (6): T gets its final distance 10 via E
steps.body:
- $d(G) = 6+2 = 8$, pred G = E
- $d(T) = 6+4 = 10$, pred T = **E**

This is the decisive update: T's distance is now 10 with predecessor E.

steps.title: Extract D (7): D→T also gives 10 — a tie, so no update
steps.body:
- via D, E would get $7+1 = 8 > 6$ — no change
- via D, T would get $7+3 = 10$, **equal** to the current $10$ → not strictly shorter, T keeps predecessor E (so SDT and SBDT, both of length 10, are never reported)
- $d(F) = 7+5 = 12$

steps.title: Finish and follow the predecessors back from T
steps.body: G (8) gives T $8+3 = 11 > 10$ — no change; then T (10) and F (12) are extracted. Following predecessors: $T \leftarrow E \leftarrow C \leftarrow A \leftarrow S$, i.e. **SACET** with length $4+1+1+4 = 10$.

optionAnalysis.reason: SDT has length $7+3=10$ too, but D is extracted *after* E has already set $d(T)=10$; the tie does not replace the predecessor.
SBDT ($3+4+3=10$) would need B to become D's predecessor, but $3+4=7$ only ties D's existing distance 7.
SACDT has length $4+1+3+3=11$; it is not even a shortest path.
E is extracted at distance 6 before D (7), and sets $d(T)=10$ first; later ties do not override it.

cse-2012-cs-40.shortcut: Shortest distance to T is 10 via several paths. With strict updates, Dijkstra keeps the path whose **last vertex is extracted first**: candidates' last hops are E ($d=6$), D ($d=7$) — E wins, and E's own predecessor chain is C ← A ← S.
pitfalls: Updating on ties ($\le$ instead of $<$) would make D the predecessor of T and report SDT.
Picking any shortest path — the question asks which one *this* algorithm reports.
cse-2012-cs-40.verification: Distances check out with Bellman–Ford style reasoning: $d(E) = \min(5+1, 7+1, 8+2) = 6$ and $d(T) = \min(6+4, 7+3, 8+3) = 10$, achieved first by E.

cse-2012-cs-42.approach: Simulate each policy on the 10 references with 3 frames and count faults. Fill the frames once (3 compulsory faults are common to all policies), then apply each replacement rule: FIFO evicts the oldest-loaded page, LRU the least-recently-used, OPT the page used farthest in the future.

steps.title: Compulsory faults: 1, 2, 3 fill the frames
steps.body: The first three references are to distinct pages and the frames are empty, so every policy faults 3 times. The 4th reference (2) is a hit for every policy.

steps.title: FIFO: always evict the page loaded earliest
steps.body:
- 4: evict 1 (oldest) — fault
- 1: evict 2 — fault
- 3: hit
- 2: evict 3 — fault
- 4, 1: hits

FIFO $= 3 + 3 = 6$ faults.

steps.title: LRU: evict the page unused for the longest time
steps.body:
After $1,2,3,2$: recency order (oldest→newest) is $1,3,2$.

- 4: evict 1 → $\{4,2,3\}$ F
- 1: evict 3 → F
- 3: evict 2 → F
- 2: evict 4 → F
- 4: evict 1 → F
- 1: evict 3 → F

Every reference after the 4th faults: LRU $= 3 + 6 = 9$.

steps.title: OPT: evict the page needed farthest in the future
steps.body:
- 4 (frames 1,2,3): next uses are 1 at ref 6, 3 at ref 7, 2 at ref 8 → evict **2** — fault
- 1, 3: hits
- 2 (frames 1,4,3): 4 at ref 9, 1 at ref 10, 3 never → evict **3** — fault
- 4, 1: hits

OPT $= 3 + 2 = 5$ faults.

optionAnalysis.reason: LRU (9) is worse than FIFO (6) on this string, not better.
OPT = 5 but FIFO = 6 — FIFO pays one extra fault (evicting 2 just before it is needed).

cse-2012-cs-42.shortcut: The tail $4,1,3,2,4,1$ cycles through 4 distinct pages with only 3 frames — the classic worst case for LRU, which then faults on every reference. OPT is always the minimum, so only FIFO needs a real simulation.
pitfalls: Treating a hit as 'refreshing' a page under FIFO — FIFO order depends only on load time.
Forgetting the 3 compulsory faults when counting.
cse-2012-cs-42.verification: The frame-by-frame simulations (shown in the canvas, computed by the same rules) give exactly 6, 9 and 5 faults.
